unit.title: Materials: properties and changes
unit.blurb: Melting, boiling, conductors, dissolving and chemical reactions – how materials behave and change.

O1.t: Describe solids, liquids and gases using the particle model, and use melting point and boiling point as properties of a substance.

O2.t: Read a thermometer, and tell the difference between evaporation and boiling.

O3.t: Name good thermal and electrical conductors and insulators, and explain how conduction moves heat.

O4.t: Plan a fair test of insulators and use the results to choose the best material.

O5.t: Describe dissolving as a reversible change and use the words solute, solvent and solution.

O6.t: Investigate how temperature changes the time a solute takes to dissolve.

O7.t: Identify chemical reactions from evidence, name reactants and products, and know most reactions are irreversible.

captions: Hello, scientists!
This is lesson 2.1: properties of substances.
Everything around us is made of tiny particles.
In a solid, like ice, the particles are packed tightly and only wobble.
In a liquid, like water, they slide past each other.
In a gas, like steam, they move fast and spread out in all directions.
When we heat ice, it melts and turns into water.
The temperature at which a solid melts is called its melting point.
Ice melts at zero degrees Celsius.
Chocolate melts at about thirty-four degrees, which is why it melts in your hand!
If we keep heating water, it starts to boil.
Big bubbles of gas form inside the liquid, and steam rises.
The temperature at which a liquid boils is its boiling point.
Pure water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
Pause and think. At what temperature does pure water boil?
Different substances melt and boil at different temperatures.
Ice melts at zero degrees.
Chocolate melts at about thirty-four degrees.
Candle wax melts at about sixty degrees.
So melting point and boiling point are properties of a substance. They help us to identify it.
Have you seen a puddle disappear on a sunny day?
The water did not boil. It evaporated.
Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature.
Boiling happens all through the liquid, and only at the boiling point.
Your turn. How is evaporation different from boiling?
Scientists measure temperature with a thermometer, in degrees Celsius.
Put the bulb in the liquid, and wait until the red line stops moving.
Read the scale with your eyes level with the top of the line.
And always take care with hot water: ask an adult to help.
Here is a graph of water being heated.
The temperature rises steadily.
At one hundred degrees the line goes flat.
While the water boils, the temperature stays the same, even though we keep heating it.
Gases are substances too.
A gas has no fixed shape. It spreads out to fill its container.
Gases can be squashed into a smaller space, like the air in a bicycle pump.
And gases have mass. A balloon full of air is heavier than an empty one.
Let's remember.
Particles are packed closely in solids and spread out in gases.
Melting point and boiling point are properties of a substance.
Water melts at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
Evaporation happens at the surface, at any temperature.
Great work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Welcome back, scientists!
This is lesson 2.2: thermal and electrical conductors.
Put a metal spoon into a cup of hot tea.
After a minute, the handle feels warm.
Heat has travelled along the spoon, from the hot end to the cold end.
This is called conduction.
The particles at the hot end start to vibrate faster.
They bump into the particles next to them, and pass the energy along.
Step by step, the heat moves through the material.
Materials that let heat pass through easily are thermal conductors. Metals are good thermal conductors.
Materials that do not let heat pass through easily are thermal insulators, like wood, plastic and wool.
Look at this saucepan.
The pan is made of metal, so heat passes quickly to the food.
The handle is plastic or wood, so it stays cool and safe to hold.
Pause and think. Why is a saucepan handle made of plastic, not metal?
Electricity can flow through some materials too.
Let's test materials in a circuit with a gap.
When we put a metal paper clip in the gap, the lamp lights. Metal is an electrical conductor.
When we use a plastic ruler, the lamp stays off. Plastic is an electrical insulator.
Electrical wires are made of copper, a very good conductor.
They are covered with plastic, an insulator, to keep us safe from electric shocks.
Never touch bare wires or play near sockets.
Your turn. Which will make the lamp light: a copper wire, or a rubber band?
Here is a fair test.
We pour the same amount of hot water into a metal cup, a plastic cup and a foam cup.
We measure the temperature every five minutes.
The water that cools most slowly is in the best insulator.
Look at the results.
The water in the metal cup cooled fastest.
The foam cup kept the water hottest, so foam is the best thermal insulator here.
Let's remember.
Conduction moves heat through a material.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.
Wood, plastic and wool are insulators.
We choose materials because of their properties.
Well done! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello again, scientists!
This is lesson 2.3: reversible changes.
Ice melts into water. If we freeze the water, we get ice again.
A change that can be undone is called a reversible change.
Melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are all reversible changes.
Now stir some sugar into water.
The sugar seems to disappear, but it is still there. The water tastes sweet!
The sugar has dissolved. Its particles have spread out between the water particles.
The mixture is called a solution.
The substance that dissolves is the solute.
The liquid it dissolves in is the solvent.
Together they make a solution. A solution looks clear and the same all the way through.
Pause and think. In salty water, which is the solute, and which is the solvent?
Dissolving is a reversible change.
If we leave salty water in a warm place, the water evaporates.
Salt crystals are left behind in the dish.
This is how people collect sea salt.
Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water or cold water?
In hot water, the particles move faster.
They bump into the sugar more often and carry it away quickly.
So sugar dissolves faster in hot water.
Your turn. Why does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?
Let's plan a fair test.
We change only one thing: the temperature of the water.
We keep the same amount of water and sugar, and we stir the same way. We measure the time the sugar takes to dissolve.
And we repeat each test, to make our results more reliable.
Here are the results.
The hotter the water, the shorter the time.
Our prediction was correct: sugar dissolves faster in hotter water.
Let's remember.
A reversible change can be undone.
A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution.
Evaporating the water gets the solute back.
And sugar dissolves faster in hot water.
Great job! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, scientists!
This is lesson 2.4: chemical reactions.
Watch a candle burn.
The wax melts. That part is a reversible change, because the wax can set again.
But the wick and the wax also burn, and make new substances: smoke, soot, water and carbon dioxide.
We cannot turn these back into a candle.
When substances react together to make new substances, we call it a chemical reaction.
The substances we start with are the reactants.
The new substances that are made are the products.
Most chemical reactions are irreversible: they cannot be undone.
Pause and think. What do we call the new substances made in a chemical reaction?
How can we tell a chemical reaction has happened? We look for evidence.
Bubbles of a new gas may form.
The colour may change.
The temperature may go up or down.
Or there may be light, a smell or a sound.
Let's try a safe reaction.
Add baking soda to vinegar.
It fizzes! Bubbles of carbon dioxide gas are made.
The reactants are vinegar and baking soda. One of the products is carbon dioxide.
Chemical reactions happen all around us.
An iron nail left in damp air goes rusty. Iron, water and oxygen react to make rust.
Cooking an egg is a reaction too. The egg changes and cannot be turned back into a raw egg.
Your turn. Is rusting a reversible change, or an irreversible change?
Here is an experiment to catch the gas.
Put some vinegar in a bottle, and some baking soda inside a balloon.
Stretch the balloon over the bottle neck, then tip the soda in.
The balloon fills up with carbon dioxide gas. That is our evidence!
Let's remember.
A chemical reaction makes new substances.
Reactants react together to make products.
Bubbles, a colour change and a temperature change are evidence of a reaction.
And most chemical reactions are irreversible.
Fantastic work! See you in the practice room.
